title: America is still beating China in the AI race
gist: The U.S. still leads China in AI on models, compute, and revenue, but recent Chinese progress (Z.ai's GLM-5.3 nearly matching Anthropic's Mythos 5 on one cybersecurity benchmark) overstates the real gap since America's true frontier models are held back from public release, and Trump-administration immigration policy pushing out Chinese AI talent is a real risk to the U.S. lead.

themes.theme: Why the U.S.-China AI gap matters beyond economics

insights.claim: AI-driven cyberwarfare lacks a mutually-assured-destruction dynamic like nuclear weapons: if one country's AI models become decisively better at hacking, the other has no proportionate retaliation option (e.g., the U.S. couldn't 'launch nukes' in response to an AI-enabled attack on its banking system, nor hack back effectively if its own AI is outclassed).
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames AI capability leadership as a potential decisive, asymmetric lever in great-power competition — relevant to how investors should price geopolitical tail risk around U.S.-China AI parity or reversal.
insights.quote: AI hacking doesn't have mutually assured destruction, like nuclear warfare does.

insights.claim: Smith predicts China is more likely to agree to cooperate with the U.S. on AI safety guardrails if U.S. AI capabilities are comfortably and visibly ahead, given the Chinese Communist Party's power-seeking orientation.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Implies that maintaining a clear U.S. AI lead is a precondition for eventual bilateral AI-safety cooperation, not an obstacle to it — relevant to how policymakers and investors should read U.S. export-control and compute-restriction strategy.
insights.quote: it seems much more likely that China would agree to cooperate on AI safety if U.S. capabilities were comfortably ahead.

insights.claim: The recent AI agent-swarm attack on Hugging Face is cited as evidence that AI has already reached a level where it can pose a significant hazard to companies and organizations, and potentially to human society.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reinforces urgency around AI-safety cooperation as a shared risk, independent of the competitive race framing.

themes.theme: The real U.S.-China model gap is wider than headlines suggest

insights.claim: The U.S. is still ahead of China in AI, with better models, more compute, and far more revenue, per Smith's assessment, though he flags the Trump administration could squander this lead — particularly by pushing Chinese AI talent out of the country.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A base-case bullish view on continued U.S. AI leadership, paired with a specific, actionable policy risk (immigration/talent policy) to monitor as a potential catalyst for erosion of that lead.
insights.quote: Fortunately, the U.S. is still beating China in the AI race. Our companies have better models, more compute, and far more revenue.

insights.claim: China's Z.ai claimed its open-source GLM-5.3 model scored 84.5% on CyberGym (identifying and confirming security vulnerabilities), narrowly ahead of Anthropic's Mythos 5 at 83.8% — though the results are self-reported and not independently verified.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The headline 'China caught up' cybersecurity benchmark claim is narrow (one metric, unverified) and should not be read as broad model parity.
insights.quote: Z.ai said GLM-5.3 scored 84.5% on CyberGym...That was slightly higher than the 83.8% it reported for Mythos 5.

insights.claim: On other benchmarks Mythos 5 remained clearly ahead of GLM-5.3: 78.0% vs. 54.4% on ExploitBench (converting flaws into working attacks), and completing 181/247 timed attack-development tasks (2hr/6hr windows) versus GLM-5.3's 105/130.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Provides the fuller benchmark picture that undercuts the 'China closing the AI gap' narrative built on a single cherry-picked metric.
insights.quote: GLM-5.3 lagged behind Mythos 5 in converting discovered flaws into working attacks...Mythos 5 completed 181 and 247 tasks, respectively.
insights.locator: paragraph with ExploitBench and timed-task data

insights.claim: The publicly-compared Mythos 5 is not actually Anthropic's best model: the original Mythos finished training in January and was released internally in February, months before the public 'Mythos Preview' came out in April — itself four months before GLM-5.3 — and Anthropic has stated it holds internal models better than Mythos, delaying releases for cybersecurity-risk reasons.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reveals that comparisons of China's fast-follower models against the U.S.'s publicly released models systematically understate the true U.S. capability lead, since top U.S. labs sit on more capable unreleased models for safety reasons — a key adjustment factor for assessing the real state of the AI race.
insights.quote: Anthropic has stated that it has internal models that are better than Mythos.

insights.claim: Smith notes earlier moments (the 'DeepSeek Moment' in early 2025, Moonshot's Kimi K3 in July, Z.ai's GLM-5.3) each generated a wave of belief that Chinese frontier models were catching up to America's, a recurring pattern in the discourse.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Useful pattern-recognition for investors: 'China catches up' narratives recur episodically around individual model releases and should be checked against fuller benchmark data and release-timing context before being priced in.
